usage_notes.narrative: O'Rourke classifies maj7 (and its extensions such as C6, CMaj9) within the Major harmonic family -- one of three families that every chord must belong to. The Major family is the I chord of the ii-V-I progression and drives the selection of major-cadence voicings from the chord dictionary. Chapter 2, p. 33.

For major chords, O'Rourke prescribes selecting a voicing from the Major ii-V-I chord collection, indexed by three inputs: the melody string (1st or 2nd), the chord type (major), and the melody note's interval relative to that chord. The collection covers every diatonic interval as the top note so any melody note can be harmonized: 'Which means: no matter which note is in the melody line, you can harmonize it by referring to the chord collection.' Chapter 2, p. 35; Chapter 4, p. 114.

O'Rourke prescribes dropping notes from major voicings in priority order when the full shape is unplayable: 'Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th. Note though that even the 3rd and the 7th can be omitted for more complex chords in certain situations as well.' The 5th is the first candidate to cut because its absence does not destroy the chord's essential character. Chapter 2, p. 79.

O'Rourke provides Major ii-V-I chord collections in two string-set variants -- string set 4321 and string set 5432 -- to match wherever the melody sits on the top two strings. The arranger selects the variant whose highest string corresponds to the string carrying the melody note at that moment. Chapter 8, pp. 266-269.

O'Rourke codifies the Tritone Substitution Rule universally: 'You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone away from the root of the original chord.' This applies to major chords, justified by shared guide tones (3rd and 7th swap places between the two chords). Chapter 7, p. 220.

O'Rourke prescribes that the I major chord can be replaced by the vi chord of the key: 'Rule: you can replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord of the key.' This is grounded in the relative-key relationship -- shared key signature means shared harmonic context. Chapter 7, p. 224.

O'Rourke prescribes a second major-to-minor substitution: 'Rule: you can substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key.' Together with the I-to-vi rule, this pair gives two licensed major-to-minor reharmonization moves for the I chord. Chapter 7, p. 225.

O'Rourke's fifth substitution rule applies to all chord qualities including major: 'Melodic common tone substitution rule: substitute any chord for another chord, as long as the new chord has a note in common with it that you use as the melody note on top.' The melody note on top of the replacement chord must be a note the original chord also contains. Chapter 7, p. 247.

O'Rourke prescribes that major (and all) chord voicings are placed on the first melody note of each bar and at chord changes, not on every melody note: 'In fact, less is more -- placing chords at key places "here and there" is easier on the hands and is usually more than enough to imply the harmony beneath the melody line.' Chapter 4, pp. 113, 122.

For solo-guitar arranging, O'Rourke prescribes the shell voicing as the irreducible minimum for major chords: root, 3rd, and 7th only, with the 5th dropped first: 'These are called shell voicings -- i.e. the "bare bones" of what you need to define the sound of the chord: the root, 3rd, and 7th.' The 6th may substitute for the 7th for a warmer, more resolved color. Chapter 5, pp. 145-147.

O'Rourke prescribes using substitutions and color additions to major chords only occasionally, not as a default density: 'Keeping things simple most of the time and just adding a substitution occasionally to brighten up the arrangement is the approach I find works best -- a good arrangement is all about subtlety!' Chapter 7, p. 222.

O'Rourke classifies min7 within the Minor harmonic family, specifically the 'm7 sub-family' (as distinct from the m7b5 sub-family): 'Minor: "m7" sub-family -- e.g. Cm7, Cm9, Cm13.' The m7 sub-family functions as the ii chord in the major ii-V-I progression and drives selection of major-cadence minor voicings. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes that min7 voicings (as the ii chord in a major context) are selected from the Major ii-V-I chord collections on string sets 4321 and 5432, indexed by melody string, chord type, and melody-note interval relative to that chord. The collection is structured so every diatonic interval can appear on top. Chapter 2, p. 35; Chapter 8, pp. 266-269.

For min7 voicings, O'Rourke prescribes the same omittable-notes priority as all chord types: drop the 5th first, then root, 11th, 9th, with 3rd and 7th as last-resort omissions in complex voicings. Chapter 2, p. 79.

O'Rourke prescribes using a min7 chord built from the 5th of any dominant chord as a substitution for that dominant: 'You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that belongs to the dominant chord). For example: an F7 chord's 5th interval is C. So you could play Cm7 over F7 to get an interesting sound.' This is borrowed from Pat Martino's minor conversion concept. Chapter 7, p. 230.

For solo-guitar arranging, O'Rourke prescribes the shell voicing as the primitive for min7 chords: root, 3rd, and 7th only, built on the 6th string root, with the 5th omitted. Shell voicings are the structural backbone of O'Rourke's solo-guitar comping vocabulary. Chapter 5, pp. 145-147; Chapter 8, p. 280.

O'Rourke's back-cycling rule licenses inserting additional minor chords from the circle of fourths before the target chord: 'Back cycling substitution rule -- you can add chords to the chord progression of a song based on the "back cycle", i.e. the circle of fourths.' This applies universally including to minor chord slots. Chapter 7, p. 243.

O'Rourke's Tritone Substitution Rule applies universally to any chord: 'You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone away from the root of the original chord.' This includes min7 chords in the ii position of the ii-V-I, where a tritone-root replacement can produce interesting reharmonization color. Chapter 7, p. 220.

O'Rourke's melodic common-tone substitution rule applies to min7 chords: 'Substitute any chord for another chord, as long as the new chord has a note in common with it that you use as the melody note on top.' This is the rule that produces modern Rosenwinkel/Kreisberg-style colors and applies to any chord quality in the arrangement. Chapter 7, p. 247.

O'Rourke classifies min7b5 within the Minor harmonic family as the 'm7b5 sub-family' (distinct from the m7 sub-family): '"m7b5" sub-family -- e.g. Cm7b5, Cm11b5.' It functions as the ii chord in a minor ii-V-i cadence, and this sub-family distinction is what drives selection of minor-cadence voicings (with b5 and b9 alterations) over major-cadence voicings. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes selecting min7b5 voicings from the Minor ii-V-i chord collections (string set 4321 and string set 5432), which carry the b5 and b9 alterations characteristic of the minor cadence. The minor sub-family distinction specifically determines that the minor dictionary section -- not the major dictionary section -- is consulted. Chapter 2, pp. 34; Chapter 8, pp. 272-275.

For min7b5 voicings, O'Rourke prescribes the universal omittable-notes priority: 5th (already altered to b5), root, 11th, 9th first -- with 3rd and 7th as last-resort omissions in complex voicings. Chapter 2, p. 79.

O'Rourke classifies dom7 (and its extensions C9, C13) within the Dominant harmonic family, specifically the 'natural dominant' or '7' sub-family (as distinct from the altered '7alt' sub-family): '"7" or "natural dominant" sub-family -- e.g. C7, C9, C13.' The dominant family is the V chord in the ii-V-I progression. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes dominant chords as the primary target for adding extensions and tensions to produce the 'jazzy' sound in arrangements: 'The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings -- particularly to dominant chords.' The chord dictionary dedicates a separate section to tensions and extensions on dominants as the method's color resource. Chapter 4, p. 127; Chapter 8, p. 278.

O'Rourke prescribes tritone substitution as the canonical dominant-chord reharmonization: 'Tritone substitution is the process of substituting one chord for another a tritone away,' justified because C7 and F#7 share guide tones -- 'The guide tones have essentially swapped places between these two chords.' This is called 'the most useful jazz substitution.' Chapter 7, pp. 214-220.

O'Rourke prescribes substituting the iim7 from the dominant's 5th in place of the dominant itself: 'You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that belongs to the dominant chord). For example: an F7 chord's 5th interval is C. So you could play Cm7 over F7 to get an interesting sound.' Drawn from Pat Martino's minor conversion concept. Chapter 7, p. 230.

O'Rourke's back-cycling rule licenses adding dominant chords before the target chord by moving backward through the circle of fourths: 'Back cycling substitution rule -- you can add chords to the chord progression of a song based on the "back cycle", i.e. the circle of fourths.' Root movement by a 4th is described as 'the most common root movement in Western music.' Chapter 7, pp. 237-243.

For dominant voicings, O'Rourke prescribes the universal omittable-notes priority: 5th first, then root, 11th, 9th, with 3rd and 7th (the guide tones) as last-resort omissions only in complex voicings where their absence is contextually safe. Chapter 2, p. 79.

For solo-guitar arranging, O'Rourke prescribes the shell voicing as the irreducible minimum for dominant chords: root, 3rd, and 7th only, built on the 6th string root, derived from bar chords by dropping the 5th first. The 6th can substitute for the 7th for a warmer, more resolved color. Extensions are stacked from the shell voicing extensions catalog. Chapter 5, pp. 145-147; Chapter 8, pp. 280-281.

O'Rourke imposes an explicit restraint rule on all dominant substitutions: 'Keeping things simple most of the time and just adding a substitution occasionally to brighten up the arrangement is the approach I find works best -- a good arrangement is all about subtlety!' Substitutions are for occasional color, not density. Chapter 7, p. 222.

O'Rourke prescribes selecting natural dominant voicings from the Major ii-V-I chord collections (string sets 4321 and 5432), indexed by melody string, chord type (dominant), and melody-note interval relative to that chord. The natural dominant sub-family determines the major-cadence collection is the correct lookup source -- not the minor-cadence collection. Chapter 2, pp. 34-35; Chapter 8, pp. 266-269.

O'Rourke classifies altered dominants as the '7alt' sub-family within the Dominant harmonic family: '"7alt" or "altered dominant" sub-family -- e.g. C7(b9), C7(b13b9), C7(b5), C7alt.' The altered sub-family distinction specifically drives selection of minor-cadence ii-V-i voicings (with b5 and b9 alterations) rather than major-cadence voicings. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes that altered dominant voicings are drawn from the dedicated 'Tensions and Extensions on Dominant Chords' section of the chord dictionary (Chapter 8, p. 278) -- a separate catalog from the natural dominant voicings -- and from the minor ii-V-i collections on string sets 4321 and 5432, which carry the b5 and b9 alterations characteristic of altered dominants in minor cadences. Chapter 8, pp. 272-278.

O'Rourke identifies altered/extended dominants as the method's primary color resource: 'The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings -- particularly to dominant chords.' Alterations such as b9, b13, and b5 are the specific tools for this color. The chapter-8 tensions-and-extensions dictionary section is the authorized lookup for these voicings. Chapter 4, p. 127; Chapter 8, p. 278.

O'Rourke includes dom7(b9) explicitly within the altered dominant sub-family: 'C7(b9)' is given as a canonical example of the '7alt' sub-family. Its selection from the minor ii-V-i dictionary sections (with the b9 alteration characteristic of minor cadences) distinguishes it from natural dominant voicings. Chapter 2, p. 34.

O'Rourke prescribes drawing dom7(b9) voicings from the Minor ii-V-i chord collections (string sets 4321 and 5432), which encode the b9 alteration characteristic of minor cadence dominants. The minor collection sections in Chapter 8 (pp. 272-275) are the authorized lookup source for this chord type. Chapter 8, pp. 272-275.

O'Rourke's Three Harmonic Families taxonomy places min-maj7 within the Minor family by chord quality. While not named explicitly as a named example in the taxonomy listing (p. 33), the minor sub-family structure (m7 and m7b5) and the minor ii-V-i collections accommodate it as part of the minor harmonic family context. O'Rourke does not address min-maj7 as a distinct chord type beyond this family placement. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.
